poem:
Week four of the strike, and Highland Valley's ore sits still,
while Codelco's ledger brags 42,100 tonnes beyond the mill.
Blame Mercury's retrograde for the muddled assays, I say,
but sulphur's the sly one, squeezing acid through the copper days.
New tonnes need permits more than picks, so this old rat keeps waiting,
for the ground holds its treasure while the paperwork goes debating.
quick_world: Iran's third strike on US targets in Bahrain ended a two-month lull and drew US retaliation, while an attack on an ADNOC vessel in Hormuz left one crew member missing, and the wires treat these as separate events with shipping impact still unclear. Trump arrived in China for a trilateral summit with Xi and Putin, and in Manila he discussed military aid and nuclear power with Marcos, so the Gulf and great-power talks now share the same news cycle. quick_mining: Highland Valley Copper in British Columbia has been ordered to stop using replacement workers to do the jobs of striking employees, which raises the risk of a longer stoppage at one of Canada's largest copper mines. Chile's copper output is nearing a 23-year low, and the Gulf sulphur and diesel shock would hit leach copper and HPAL nickel costs before it reduces any tonnes. Canuc's new gold zone at East Sudbury, with 2.99 g/t over 8.0 metres, is a useful exploration signal in a market where drilling is still going mainly to gold.
sections: Industry health

Concentrate is tight. Negative treatment charges are deepening, smelters are being paid to take feed, and Chile's biggest quarterly economic drop since 2020 shows the mining slump reaching the national accounts.

Juniors are drilling again, but the 38% rise in gold exploration budgets comes from a promotional source. Drill releases are running about two to one gold over copper, so gold is pulling the rigs while new copper moves slowly. Freeport's notes fund the balance sheet, and Grasberg's recovery will be judged by block cave and mill rates, not by the bond issue.
Regional trends

North America: The Hawaii federal ruling against the Pacific seabed plan is a legal signal, not a tonnage story. It comes from the desk's review and is not in my wire reading, so treat its details as provisional. Ottawa's up-to-C$14M offer for the Yukon tungsten project and its backing for Mactung are policy support, and tonnes are years away. Nevada exploration notices are steady.

Latin America: Colombia is becoming a copper district on the back of AngloGold Ashanti's roughly US$2.5bn plan and Collective's US$100M for 2027, and both depend on permits. Chile's output weakness is now a macro story, and Brazil's objection to the EU review of Anglo's nickel sale to MMG adds a trade-policy dispute to the nickel picture.

Middle East and Asia: The Gulf is an active conflict, with the Bahrain strike and the Hormuz vessel attack confirmed by wire reports. The Kuwait and Qeshm reports remain unconfirmed. Indonesia's state-share push has no decree yet, and Mongolia's leadership change adds political risk to Oyu Tolgoi.
Technology & demand

Nickel and cobalt are losing ground to LFP and sodium-ion grid storage, and lithium faces a long-run sodium-ion threat even though grid storage still adds lithium demand today. The timing is low confidence and the direction is medium confidence. Rare earths and tungsten gain from the Aclara NdPr step and the Western tungsten policy support.

Copper's grid case holds, but I'm downgrading the claim that AI data-centre demand pulls copper directly. The Nvidia chip-shipment halt to China weakens that link, while transformers and grid upgrades still run on domestic and allied demand.
On the horizon

The US deep-sea lease sale later this month is the next test of the Hawaii ruling. If the sale proceeds anyway, the legal challenge becomes the story and the court's reasoning is what other federal mineral leasing will face.

Diesel and sulphur are the cost signals to watch over the next one to three months. Diesel reaches North American haul fleets and reagent freight first, and sulphur reprices SX-EW and HPAL acid on contract cycles.

The Trump trip to China, the trilateral with Xi and Putin, and APEC in Shenzhen will show whether China issues multi-year export licences for antimony, tungsten and rare earths. Those licences would restore flow but would not change copper's tightness at the smelter, grid, and permit steps.
creative: The Gulf sulphur shock would hit copper and nickel through the same reagent channel, since Chilean SX-EW and Indonesian HPAL both depend on sulphuric acid. A single sulphur spike could tighten both metals at once, which would make the two look more correlated than their demand drivers suggest. (speculation level: medium)

If Western chip controls slow China's AI buildout, China may redirect state spending into grid and transmission, which would keep Chinese copper demand firm while the US data-centre pull weakens. (speculation level: high)

Governments are becoming the development lenders. Ottawa, Kazakhstan, Brazil and Norway are all funding projects that the junior market no longer finances reliably, so the question for North American mining is whether state money turns into dated permits and offtake, not whether it arrives. (speculation level: low)
global_view:
The most direct mining risk is the Gulf. Iran's third strike on US targets in Bahrain ended a two-month lull, and an attack on an ADNOC vessel in Hormuz left a crew member missing. AP and Reuters report these as separate events, and I can't tell from the headlines how far shipping has been disrupted. The mining link is sulphur and diesel. Sulphur becomes sulphuric acid for leach copper in Chile, Zambia and the DRC, and for HPAL nickel in Indonesia. Costs would move before tonnes do.

US-China is the second driver. Trump has arrived in China for a trilateral with Xi and Putin, and Xi is pressing for freer trade at APEC ahead of the Shenzhen meeting. Trump has also discussed military aid and nuclear power with Marcos in Manila. For mining, the test is whether these talks produce multi-year export licences for antimony, tungsten and rare earths. Separately, Nvidia's halt on shipping US-approved AI chips to China and the reported spy scandal could slow China's AI buildout. That would weaken one pull on grid and data-centre demand, though the effect on copper is speculative.

Africa: a US-backed "mineral highway" for DR Congo is being promoted (BBC). It is a headline with no detail, but if it is built, it would change cobalt and copper trade routes. Alaska's Senate seat going to a Democrat has no direct permitting effect yet.

discussions.strategist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
Labour is still copper's binding constraint. A Canadian order barring Highland Valley from using replacement workers is the most important North American development today. It makes a negotiated settlement more likely than a long wait, though it sets no date. Chile shows the supply squeeze: reported output is nearing a 23-year low. Capital is returning anyway. Gabriela Mistral's US$866M extension cleared an environmental hurdle, AngloGold is committing about US$2.5bn to a Colombian copper mine, Southern Copper has begun early works at El Pilar, and Sumitomo says it wants more copper investment. Tonnes from these projects are years away. A China report that concentrate-fed smelting capacity nears a 2026 ceiling is a reminder that more ore does not help if smelters are full.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
- North America: Ottawa offered up to C$14M for the Yukon tungsten project and backed Fireweed's Mactung, and Canada widened tariff relief on Chinese metals. Money is now flowing alongside permits. In the US, a federal court ruled the administration broke the law in approving the American Samoa deep-sea lease sale. That casts doubt on the November timing the desk had recorded. Permitting is moving in pockets: a North Carolina lithium project received a state air permit, and Utah saw 141 "Alice" claims filed on BLM land. The Boundary Waters fight shows permitting reform remains contested.
- Latin America: Brazil is contesting the EU's review of Anglo's nickel sale to China's MMG, a sign that foreign-ownership scrutiny is spreading. Panama has authorised restart talks with First Quantum, which is a process step, not a timetable. Drilling in Ecuador and Colombia is copper-gold.
- Africa: Guinea's push to keep gold at home is disrupting exports. Major miners are stockpiling bullion, tying up working capital, and more than 220 people have been jailed in the crackdown. In the DRC, Barrick's furlough of Congo mine staff over Ebola concerns shows health shutdowns can idle output as fast as a walkout.
- Asia: Mongolia's president resigned over alleged corruption, adding policy risk to Oyu Tolgoi.
- Exploration: junior drilling is dominated by gold (Goldboro, Sudbury, Ontario's Timmins camp), with uranium in Sweden. Single-outlet reports from Guinea and Mongolia are thin, so treat the counts with caution.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Grid: transformer shortage warnings and local fights over data-centre transport and permitting show the AI power build outrunning equipment. That supports copper and electrical steel, and is among the more durable demand drivers on the desk.
- Batteries: Mercedes' cobalt-free goal for 2030 is intent, not tonnes. AceOn's 12V sodium-ion range mainly replaces lead-acid in starter-type roles, so it trims little lithium. Battery recycling and India's hold-back on discarded batteries add secondary nickel, cobalt and lithium supply.
- Tungsten: Canadian federal money is partly defence-linked, which makes it stickier than pure policy.

ON THE HORIZON:
- Highland Valley: a signed deal is the trigger; restart follows over weeks to months.
- Trump's Asia trip and the Carney–Xi meeting: whether China publishes multi-year export licence terms for tungsten, antimony and rare earths.
- American Samoa: whether the court ruling halts the lease sale.
- Guinea: whether export rules and expulsions ease.
- Chile: the private-role decision and an explanation of the 42,100-tonne overstatement.
- What would change my view: a quick Highland Valley deal would ease the labour constraint faster than I expect. Chinese licence terms would move critical-minerals policy from intent to tonnes. Chile output staying near its low would point to a deeper shortfall.
discussions.geologist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
Copper's near-term picture is getting more fragile. A report that Chile's copper output is near a 23-year low, on top of the Codelco overstatement and the Highland Valley strike, points to existing mines struggling rather than new tonnes arriving. A BC labour ruling ordering Highland Valley to stop using replacement workers raises pressure on the company to settle, but even a signed deal means weeks to months before the mine restarts. Barrick's furlough of Congo staff over Ebola is another reminder that health shutdowns can idle African output as fast as a walkout. Capital is still moving toward copper: AngloGold's roughly US$2.5bn Colombia copper plan, Sumitomo's search for copper assets, and Southern Copper's early works at El Pilar. Junior drilling is concentrated in gold, in Nova Scotia (NexGold's high-grade RC intercepts at Goldboro), Sudbury (Canuc's new zone), Ecuador (Auro's 679.9m at 0.44 g/t gold) and Nevada.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
North America: Ottawa's offer of up to C$14M for the Yukon tungsten project and its backing for Fireweed's Mactung show critical-minerals money turning into tungsten projects. Perpetua's US$55.5M deal for US tungsten supply and Canada's wider tariff relief on Chinese metals point the same way. In the US, a court ruling that the American Samoa deep-sea lease sale broke the law weakens the November timing I flagged earlier. Alaska's Nova Minerals secured final antimony permits, and Utah's 141 Alice claims and two new Nevada exploration notices show staking still running. Mexico's two permitted projects moving toward construction are a modest positive.
Latin America: Panama's authorisation of formal Cobre Panama talks is the first real movement, but there is still no timetable. Chile's Gabriela Mistral life extension cleared approval.
Africa: Guinea's PDI Gold permits are a formal-supply story for later. The near-term squeeze is on artisanal gold, with reports of expulsions and jailings. Wires give Perenti's Geita contract as US$67M, US$670M and US$675M, so treat its size as unsettled.
Asia: Mongolia's president's resignation adds policy risk to Oyu Tolgoi, which depends on China-facing exports.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
Grid equipment is where the AI buildout pulls hardest on copper and electrical steel. Johns Hopkins warns of transformer shortages, and a Hobart data-centre transformer shipment was stopped by a county over road use. Those are logistics and permitting bottlenecks, not metal scarcity, but they slow the copper demand arriving. LFP grid storage keeps taking share from nickel and cobalt, and Mercedes' cobalt-free target for 2030 pushes the same way. Sodium-ion's 12V launch is early but takes small-format demand from lithium. India's black mass export ban and Veolia's French recycling plant add secondary nickel, cobalt and lithium. Tungsten and antimony gain from defence-linked money.

ON THE HORIZON:
- Highland Valley: a signed deal, then restart timing. A replacement-worker ruling makes an early settlement more likely.
- American Samoa: any appeal, and whether the November lease sale proceeds.
- Cobre Panama: whether talks produce a dated timetable.
- Trump's Asia trip: whether China publishes multi-year export licence terms for antimony, tungsten and rare earths.
- Guinea: whether export rules and expulsions ease.
Would change my view: a Highland Valley deal within weeks, Codelco stating the basis of its overstatement, or Chilean output data confirming the decline.
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your restart point sharpens my view. I treated a signed Highland Valley deal as the trigger, but you're right that it starts a lag. A concentrator that has sat idle doesn't restart overnight, so the copper relief is further off than my framing implied.

Where I'd push back is on Barrick's Congo furlough. Health shutdowns can idle output, but they tend to be episodic, so I'd weight them less as a sign of structural fragility. Your Chile reading is stronger than mine on existing mines struggling, though I'd still hold the 23-year low lightly until Codelco explains the overstatement. A bad number can make a mine look worse than it is, or the reverse.

On tungsten, I agree the defence link matters more than the policy label. I'd add that Perpetua's deal and Ottawa's money share a buyer: governments who want supply outside China. That makes these projects stickier than a price spike would.

The bigger pattern across both analyses is that capital and permits are arriving for copper and tungsten, but tonnes are years away. The flow of metal is also increasingly set by states rather than markets: Guinea's gold retention, Brazil's scrutiny of the MMG sale, China's licence terms, Mongolia's political churn. Permits and money are moving faster than output, and the smelter ceiling is a reminder that ore is not the same as metal. I'd frame the next year as a test of whether governments can turn intent into tonnes.
discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your read on labour and the Chile numbers is right, and I'd add a geological layer. A mine that is already producing can lose ore grade and tonnes over the years without any new trouble, and a 23-year low in Chile fits that pattern: aging porphyry pits working lower-grade ore. Replacing that output means new discoveries, and from discovery to production is usually 15 years or more. Capital returning to copper matters, but it can't close a gap that opens this fast.

Where I'd push back is on timing for tungsten. Ottawa's money and the Perpetua deal are real signals, but a project like Mactung has a long road of drilling, metallurgy, permits, and financing before it produces tonnes. Defence-linked money makes that road more likely to get finished, but it doesn't shorten it. I'd treat tungsten as a policy story for the next several years rather than a near-term supply story.

On Highland Valley, I agree the ruling raises pressure on a settlement. Restart speed depends on what the mill and pit looked like during the shutdown. A concentrator kept on care-and-maintenance restarts far faster than one left cold, so the length of the strike matters as much as the deal itself.

Taken together, the two analyses show a split. Money and permits are moving toward copper, tungsten, and antimony, but the tonnes that could ease the squeeze are mostly years away. Junior drilling is heavy in gold, which I read as much a sign of where financing is easy as of where the geology is best. The supply pipeline is set by today's financing, and that shapes which metals get found in five years.

chief_sessions.strategist_answer:
**On the defence-metals question:** Multi-year antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licences would matter, but they would not reorder the 12-month ranking. Licences restore flow; they don't add tonnes or fix the conversion bottleneck. Copper's tightness comes from smelting, power equipment and permits, and no export licence touches those. I would narrow the defence-metal premium somewhat, since a licence is a policy lever Beijing can pull back, and I'd treat tungsten and antimony headlines as more volatile than the copper story. Western projects like Mactung would still need years to reach tonnes, so the licence changes the urgency of policy support more than near-term supply.

On the Nvidia point, Dr Simon is right to press. A halt on AI-chip shipments to China weakens the AI-driven part of my grid-demand argument, and I should have said so. I'd still keep the grid case, because utility upgrades, transformers and renewables interconnection run on domestic and allied demand, not on Nvidia's China sales. But I'd downgrade any claim that AI data-centre demand is pulling copper directly.

**On Hormuz:** I give the sulphur channel real weight if the exchange runs into December, but diesel is the line that moves first, not sulphur. Haul fleets at North American open pits burn large volumes of diesel, and freight on reagents follows fuel within weeks. Sulphur and acid for SX-EW plants in Arizona and Nevada reprice on contract cycles, so the pass-through typically takes one to three months. Much of the Gulf's sulphur is a by-product of sour gas and refining, so a shipping disruption tightens supply quickly even though the producing capacity stays intact.

My confidence is medium. The confirmed events are the Bahrain strike and the Hormuz vessel attack. The Kuwait and Qeshm reports are desk-sourced and I'd not build a cost case on them until they're confirmed. Diesel is the signal to watch first.
chief_sessions.geologist_answer:
On the Chilean question: from what I've seen at SX-EW operations, sulphur or acid stocks are usually measured in weeks, not months. Many plants hold roughly two to four weeks of supply on site, and the number depends on shipping schedules and how the contract is structured. I'm working from experience here, not a current survey, so treat it as a range. Chile also imports much of its sulphur from Gulf producers, which is why Hormuz matters to this chain.

Curtailment would come more slowly than the stock count suggests. Leach pads hold ore and solution, so a shortage first thins the acid strength in the leach circuit. Cathode output then falls over several weeks to a few months as the pads drain down. Operators would usually protect electrowinning power and cut tonnage through the leach circuit first, so cathode losses would show up later and more gradually than an outright plant stoppage.

On Indonesian HPAL: the acid is the cheap part to replace. The hard part is the process itself. High-pressure autoclaves run near 250°C, use titanium-lined vessels, and are tuned to specific ore chemistry. Acid consumption depends on the limonite and saprolite mix, so a change in acid strength or source would hit throughput and recovery before it hit cost. Most HPAL plants make acid on site from imported sulphur, so a sulphur spike is their real exposure. Buying acid from elsewhere could be done in weeks. Changing the flowsheet or ore blend would take months, and changing the autoclaves would take years.

Dr Simon, this changes my earlier view. I had treated the Gulf as a cost story. A sustained sulphur shortage would make it a supply story for leach copper and HPAL nickel within a quarter or two, and I'd give the Hormuz channel real weight for December. The Kuwait and Qeshm strikes are desk-sourced, so I won't build on them.
chief_sessions.conclusion:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
- Concentrate is tight. Negative treatment charges are deepening, smelters are being paid to take feed, and Chile's biggest quarterly economic drop since 2020 shows the mining slump reaching the national accounts.
- Juniors are drilling again, but the 38% rise in gold exploration budgets comes from a promotional source. Drill releases are running about two to one gold over copper, so gold is pulling the rigs while new copper moves slowly. Freeport's notes fund the balance sheet, and Grasberg's recovery will be judged by block cave and mill rates, not by the bond issue.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
- North America: The Hawaii federal ruling against the Pacific seabed plan is a legal signal, not a tonnage story. It comes from the desk's review and is not in my wire reading, so treat its details as provisional. Ottawa's up-to-C$14M offer for the Yukon tungsten project and its backing for Mactung are policy support, and tonnes are years away. Nevada exploration notices are steady.
- Latin America: Colombia is becoming a copper district on the back of AngloGold Ashanti's roughly US$2.5bn plan and Collective's US$100M for 2027, and both depend on permits. Chile's output weakness is now a macro story, and Brazil's objection to the EU review of Anglo's nickel sale to MMG adds a trade-policy dispute to the nickel picture.
- Middle East and Asia: The Gulf is an active conflict, with the Bahrain strike and the Hormuz vessel attack confirmed by wire reports. The Kuwait and Qeshm reports remain unconfirmed. Indonesia's state-share push has no decree yet, and Mongolia's leadership change adds political risk to Oyu Tolgoi.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Nickel and cobalt are losing ground to LFP and sodium-ion grid storage, and lithium faces a long-run sodium-ion threat even though grid storage still adds lithium demand today. The timing is low confidence and the direction is medium confidence. Rare earths and tungsten gain from the Aclara NdPr step and the Western tungsten policy support.
- Copper's grid case holds, but I'm downgrading the claim that AI data-centre demand pulls copper directly. The Nvidia chip-shipment halt to China weakens that link, while transformers and grid upgrades still run on domestic and allied demand.

ON THE HORIZON:
- The US deep-sea lease sale later this month is the next test of the Hawaii ruling. If the sale proceeds anyway, the legal challenge becomes the story and the court's reasoning is what other federal mineral leasing will face.
- Diesel and sulphur are the cost signals to watch over the next one to three months. Diesel reaches North American haul fleets and reagent freight first, and sulphur reprices SX-EW and HPAL acid on contract cycles.
- The Trump trip to China, the trilateral with Xi and Putin, and APEC in Shenzhen will show whether China issues multi-year export licences for antimony, tungsten and rare earths. Those licences would restore flow but would not change copper's tightness at the smelter, grid, and permit steps.

CREATIVE ANGLES:
- The Gulf sulphur shock would hit copper and nickel through the same reagent channel, since Chilean SX-EW and Indonesian HPAL both depend on sulphuric acid. A single sulphur spike could tighten both metals at once, which would make the two look more correlated than their demand drivers suggest. (speculation level: medium)
- If Western chip controls slow China's AI buildout, China may redirect state spending into grid and transmission, which would keep Chinese copper demand firm while the US data-centre pull weakens. (speculation level: high)
- Governments are becoming the development lenders. Ottawa, Kazakhstan, Brazil and Norway are all funding projects that the junior market no longer finances reliably, so the question for North American mining is whether state money turns into dated permits and offtake, not whether it arrives. (speculation level: low)

GLOBAL BRIEFING:
Keep three things in mind. The Gulf conflict is now active: a sustained disruption to the Hormuz shipping route would raise sulphur and diesel costs for leach copper in Chile, Zambia and the DRC, and for HPAL nickel in Indonesia, before it reduces metal output. The US-China talks in Manila and Shenzhen decide whether antimony, tungsten and rare-earth export licences return, which matters for defence-linked metals. The Hawaii ruling against the Pacific seabed plan creates a legal test for federal mineral leasing, though no seabed tonnes are coming soon. Chip export controls may slow China's AI buildout, which weakens one data-centre pull on copper.

PREDICTION: Indonesia publishes a numeric decree setting the state-share requirement for mining companies | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
PREDICTION: China publishes multi-year export licences covering antimony or tungsten | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
